The 10,225th meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is the situation in the Middle East. The agenda is adopted. In accordance with rule 37 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the representatives of Israel, Oman, the Syrian Arab Republic, and Turkey to participate in this meeting. It is so decided.

In accordance.

With Rule 39 of the Council's Provisional Rules of Procedure, I invite the following briefers to participate in this meeting: Mr. Claudio Cordone, Deputy Special Envoy of the Secretary-General for Syria; Mr. Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator; and Mr. Yasser Tabbara, Co-founder of the Syrian Forum. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item 2 of the agenda. I now give the floor to Mr. Claudio Cordone, and I wish him a warm welcome. You have the floor.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President, in my latest stay in Syria, I have seen further progress in institutional development, while Syrians continue to grapple with dire economic conditions and the country confronts internal and external security challenges. Above all, I had the opportunity to hear from local officials and civil society in different parts of the country, a strong commitment to build a Syria where everyone feels they belong, with representative institutions, a culture of accountability for both past and present, and tangible improvements in people's lives with sustained international support. Mr. President, on 27 August, the People's Assembly announced the composition of the 26 standing committees established following last month's adoption of a comprehensive set of rules of procedure. Five of the 26 committees are chaired by women, and Syrian women interlocutors continue to seek further leadership roles in the Assembly and a commitment by all its members to meet the diverse expectations of Syrian women and those of Syrians as a whole. Throughout this week, the People's Assembly has been holding an extraordinary session to adopt its budget and start consideration of a number of laws. Notable is the abrogation yesterday of the court on terrorism. MPs have also been hearing from the Minister of Education on challenges related to access to schools. These are notable initial steps in the Assembly's developing oversight role. Last week, I met with Speaker Al-Awaq to discuss how my office can best support the Assembly, including as it establishes its administrative structure and considers multiple offers of international assistance. And I agreed with the Speaker that these offers should be well-coordinated and tailored to the needs of the Assembly. Mr. President, earlier this month, I also discussed with the Syrian authorities preparations for the holding of future parliamentary and presidential elections, and possibly other elections, in line with the new Constitution. We considered legal, political, and operational challenges for future polls, drawing on lessons from the experience of establishing the People's Assembly. The heavy lifting needed for the implementation of these electoral plans within the remaining three and a half years of the transition must not be underestimated. But I'm pleased with the developing cooperation with the Syrian authorities also in this field, including and exploring potential opportunities for UN electoral assistance. As for the drawing up of a new constitution, the inclusive, transparent and participatory nature of any process is essential if a genuine social contract and shared vision of a future state is to be forged, and we will be ready to support a Syrian-led process in this regard. Mr. President, two days after the United States removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism last month, the first international Visa and Mastercard transactions were successfully conducted in Syria. This comes alongside deeper engagement by international financial institutions and growing interests from international business. Syria is also seeking to position itself as a regional corridor for energy and trade. These moves towards economic integration are notable. And I urge donor countries to facilitate investment and economic cooperation on the understanding that these should be equitable and accompanied by strong safeguards. Ultimately, ordinary Syrians will judge economic recovery through their daily lives, jobs, affordable food and housing, functioning electricity and other basic services, and the ability to return and rebuild their lives. Yet these opportunities stand in stark contrast to the economic pressures confronting ordinary Syrians. The sharp increases in fuel prices announced last weekend triggered demonstrations and roadblocks across several parts of the country. These protests reflect the immediate impact of higher energy costs, but also wider concerns over whether economic recovery is translating into tangible improvements in people's lives, especially the poorest. Mr. President, in the past weeks, I visited Aleppo, Tartus, Latakia, and Idlib, where I met the governors and a wide range of civil society actors. Local officials illustrated encouraging developments in several areas, including steps to strengthen local governance and efforts to expand participation of different components of Syrian society in state institutions. They welcomed close cooperation with the United Nations and urged more coordination in humanitarian and recovery programming. Civil society interlocutors stressed the need for further progress on transitional justice, for women's economic and political participation, and for greater clarity on the vision for the transition. The messages from many was clear. Progress at the national level must translate into greater inclusion, security services, and economic opportunity at the local level. And I look forward to further engagement across the country with officials as well as with women and civil society. In this context, we are currently working with the government, civil society and other entities on initiatives to address the proliferation of hate speech. Mr. President, on the Northeast, we see important progress. Three days after Mazloum Abdi announced the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces and integration into the Syrian military, he was appointed as a presidential advisor. There have also been further steps on military, police, and civilian administration integration in Hasake. I am, however, concerned that a former SDF fighter was recently abducted and killed, triggering demonstrations in several Kurdish-majority towns and a standoff between General Security and some other security forces around the detention center, which some detainees then set on fire. I note that several suspects have reportedly been arrested and that investigations are continuing. And it is important that the abduction and killing are fully investigated and that those responsible are held accountable. And I welcome the efforts of senior government officials and Presidential Advisor Masloum Abdi on restoring calm. Returns also continue to take place. On 1 September, approximately 50 families displaced for more than a decade returned voluntarily from Ras al-Ayn to Al-Hasakah city in the first organized return convoy of this kind, a pilot initiative facilitated by the authorities to support and inform future returns movements in northeastern Syria. And discussions are continuing on the use of the Kurdish language. Attention continues on the future role of women who served in the women's protection units. It will be important that women who played prominent roles in the political social life of Northeastern Syria can continue to participate meaningfully in the institutions of the new Syria. Mr. President, the situation in Sweida remains deeply concerning. On 1st September, renewed clashes between internal security forces and the National Guard affiliated with Sheik Hikmat al-Hijri left several casualties. I also deplore the abduction and expulsion from Sweida on 4th September of Druze notable Atef Nadi by armed men reportedly affiliated with the National Guard. He had publicly rejected statements associating the Druze community's future with Israel and expressed his support for Syria's unity. These and other forms of repression of freedom of expression cannot provide a path forward. Following the presidential decree last month, granting students from Sweida Governorate an exceptional examination, only around 150 of approximately 14,000 eligible students participated. The examination centers were in areas under government control, specifically in some of the villages devastated during the events of July 2025. and students from within Swayed that were prevented from reaching examination centers and faced other restrictions of movement. At this point, unless these children can sit for examinations in a safe, secure, and supportive environment without pressure or disruption of movement, other solution should be considered to ensure that the right to education is upheld. And my office and UN agencies stand ready to help. I wish to take this opportunity to stress that the issue of Suwayda and the future of its Druze community must ultimately be resolved by Syrians themselves, within a united Syria and without disruptive foreign interference. I look forward to renewed efforts to reinvigorate the September 2025 roadmap, promoting the restoration of state authority while addressing the real trust deficits that followed the events of July 2025 and continued grievances within the community in Sweita. A phased but determined process could be initiated to address detainees and missing persons and support gradual, sustainable returns among confidence-building measures to build trust between the states and the Druze community and promote reconciliation between the Druze and Bedouin communities. And my office and the rest of the UN in Syria are ready to cooperate in exploring these dimensions and provide operational support while supporting mediation efforts aimed at reaching broader political and security agreements. Mr. President, Israeli presence and military activity in southern Syria has continued in violation of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement. with near daily incursions, temporary checkpoints, searches of homes, and artillery fire, particularly in Quneitra and western Daraa. Two Syrians who were taken to Israel and held there were returned home, but others remain in Israeli custody. On 9 September, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu visited Israeli forces on Jabal al-Shaykh, Mount Hermon, reiterating that Israel would not permit hostile forces to establish themselves along its border. I have taken very clear note of the statement by the Syrian Permanent Representative and 43 Member States last week in response to this other violation of Syrian sovereignty. The Secretary-General has been very clear: violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity must cease, and the 1974 agreement must be respected. Security concerns cannot be addressed in any sustainable way through unilateral military action or an open-ended military presence. Diplomacy must prevail. And I welcome in this regard the mediation efforts led by the United States aimed at reaching an understanding among Syria and its neighbors that reduces tensions and promotes sustainable security arrangements. And these must respect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity and comply fully with international law. Mr. President, I welcome the General Assembly's unanimous adoption on 1 September of a Syrian-sponsored resolution establishing 19 December as the International Day for the Recognition of Women Searchers for Missing Persons. It is an important recognition of Syrian women who have spent years seeking truth and accountability. Their experience is also a reminder that Syrian women have been among key political, civic, and social actors in this transition and must be able to participate fully in shaping its future. I also welcome Syria's cooperation with the OPCW, which has verified the destruction of material related to chemical weapons in Syria, and with the IAEA, whose Board of Governors declared on 9 September that Syria is no longer in noncompliance with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Mr. President, as attention turns to this General Assembly period, we can reinforce a simple message. Syria has made important advances, and these should be recognized and supported. At the same time, progress should create momentum for the next steps, addressing the significant challenges that persist. For the Syrian authorities, this requires strengthening accountable institutions, widening participation, protecting civil space and advancing transitional justice. For international partners, it entails sustained political and practical support for recovery, reconstruction and safe, dignified and voluntary returns. And for our part, This requires my office consolidating in Damascus to fit the growing cooperation with the Government and engagement with Syrian society, to better implement our mandate of support to the Syrian-led political transition. And the UN as a whole remains committed to develop its partnership with Syria. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Cordoni for his briefing. I now give the floor to Mr. Tom Fletcher.

Mr. President, thank you for this opportunity to brief the Council on the humanitarian situation in Syria. And thank you, as ever, to my colleague for his work. Mr. President, my briefings tend to feature many numbers, but here is the most important one. Since December 2024, more than 2 million internally displaced Syrians, 1.8 million refugees, have gone home voluntarily. This historic wave of return, the highest in Syria in decades, is a profound sign of hope. Improved security, eased sanctions, resilient communities are driving this recovery. Through 300 partners, we've reached over 2.5 million people monthly this year with humanitarian support, reopening key routes into Al-Hasakah and flights to Deir ez-Zor. in August. However, four obstacles threaten this progress: continued displacement, localised insecurity, regional escalation, and landmines. First, 5.5 million people inside Syria have not yet gone home, nearly 800,000 of them still in camps, over 75% of them women and children. And currently, only 18% of Syrians outside the country say that they plan to return home in the coming year. Without homes, schools, or clean water, today's returnees risk becoming tomorrow's displaced. So we must continue to support the government's No Tents and No Camps initiative to achieve safe return for all those who choose to go home. A second challenge, localized insecurity risks choking recovery. ISIL attacks in the east and northeast, sporadic violence, rebuilding challenges, and bureaucratic hurdles threaten lasting peace. True stability is not possible until every community, most crucially Syria's women, are fully integrated in the nation's political and economic fabric. Third, and as you've just heard, the mounting risks beyond Syria's borders. The escalation of tension across the region means maritime choke points, disrupted supply chains, reduced humanitarian access, and even greater economic pressure on Syrian families. Alongside the weeks of disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, we now face blockages in Bab al-Mandab. And for Syrians, I fear that that means increased fuel prices, freight charges, insurance premiums, procurement lead times, as well as disruptions to imports from Asia and the Gulf and to shipping through Tartus and Latakia. Higher diesel costs, up 40% only this week, will hit agricultural production, water pumping, electricity generation, bakeries and heating as winter approaches, with disproportionate consequences for displaced people and other vulnerable households. For families already struggling, high fuel and transport costs will increase the prices of food, medicine, and other essential goods. The cost of what we call a minimum expenditure basket has increased 33% since June 2025, while electricity tariffs have increased in some places by several hundred percent. And those price increases, of course, drive up the cost of our humanitarian response. A fourth challenge, mines are making recovery efforts a lethal gamble. Since December 2024, explosive ordnance has killed 880 people, including 269 children, and maimed 1,616 more, nearly 40% of them children. Mines block the fields, orchards, grazing lands that families need to feed themselves. You cannot build an economy over a minefield. So it is right that the Syrian Government has made the No Mines Initiative a centerpiece of its planning, backed by the humanitarian community. Mr. President, I close with three asks of this Council, all in pursuit of the effort to help Syrians return, rebuild, and move beyond crisis, and beyond the need for Security Council discussion. First, we must invest in the transition out of humanitarian need and towards reconstruction and growth. We should be making a collective push alongside the Syrian authorities to move through this transition in the coming year. But while humanitarian organizations continue to deliver, resources fall dramatically short of what is needed. Agencies are being forced to reduce, delay, stop activities just when families with the most severe needs need help to make the journey from displacement to recovery. Food assistance for the most vulnerable is being halved. Our hyper-prioritized appeal may be 57% funded now, but key sectors lag behind. Our food and education plans are only 26% funded. So I thank all donors who are stepping up to fund the appeal. All of this tracked in our publicly available system including the US with $297 million, the European Commission, $221 million, the UK, $46 million, Japan, $42 million, and Germany, $40 million. All those figures publicly available and many more. And I thank donors for doing so in line with the humanitarian reset. As of the end of August, the Syria Humanitarian Fund has received $325 million. over twice last year's figure. As winter approaches and the regional situation remains unstable, funding will be vital as a bulwark against losing the advances that Syria has fought so hard to achieve. If we fail to invest today, the costs will be higher tomorrow in renewed displacement, deteriorating services, and lost opportunities to consolidate stability and transition towards reconstruction and development in Syria. My second ask, remove the obstacles standing between recovery and development. We must work with the Syrian authorities to clear the mines, remove the rubble, and continue progress in unblocking administrative delays, and to fund livelihoods. Third, we must invest the political capital needed to keep Syria out of regional conflict. We must redouble diplomatic efforts in support of Syria's territorial integrity. We must take every measure so that the Syrian people are not subjected to further conflict, displacement, and chaos. Mr. President, Syrians have endured enough. They are making progress that has defied many who predicted or wished it impossible. Let us also meet this moment. Thank you.
I thank Mr. Fletcher for his briefing. I now give the floor to Mr. Yasser Tabbara.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Distinguished members of the Security Council, Thank you for the opportunity to address the Council on behalf of Syrian civil society. Syria today stands simultaneously at a moment of extraordinary possibility and of difficulty. After years of conflict, repression, displacement, and institutional erosion, Syrians are attempting not simply to rebuild a country, but to redefine the relationship between the state and its citizens. Today, I would like to focus on three dualities that will significantly shape the success of Syria's transition. The first is the perceived duality between sovereignty and international cooperation. Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity must be respected without qualification. Syrians have paid an enormous price for external interference, fragmentation, and the erosion of national sovereignty. But sovereignty should not be confused with isolation. A Syrian-led and Syrian-owned transition cannot mean that Syria must undertake every aspect of that transition alone. Our country urgently requires knowledge, expertise, investment, technology, and technical assistance. This applies particularly to transitional justice and the search for missing persons, but also to judicial reform, public administration, security sector governance, economic reform, and institution building. National ownership should therefore answer the question, who decides, not who provides. Effective sovereignty requires capable institutions, where decades of authoritarianism and years of conflict have weakened those institutions. International technical assistance can strengthen rather than diminish sovereignty. At the same time, international cooperation cannot reproduce externally designed programs detached from Syrian realities. This principle is particularly important for transitional justice, Justice must be Syrian-led, responsive to victims and families, and meaningfully include Syrian women. But Syria should also make full use of the considerable experience, evidence, and institutional knowledge accumulated internationally during the past 15 years, including by Syrian civil society. The second duality is between loyalty and trust on one hand, and qualification on the other. Every government emerging from conflict naturally seeks officials whom it trusts. Syria's recent history makes this understandable. But trust cannot become the principal qualification for public service. If Syria is to rebuild functioning institutions, competence, integrity, and merit must increasingly determine who serves in positions of leadership in public office. Allow me one very human example. For many Syrians, it's genuinely heartening to see a distinguished Syrian human rights lawyer occupying the seat of the permanent representative of the Syrian Arab Republic, Ambassador Ibrahim Alabi. But the example should lead us to a broader question. How many highly qualified Syrian experts could contribute to rebuilding the country if the correct recruitment mechanisms existed? And what institutions are we creating to ensure that the most capable Syrians can compete fairly for the positions in which they can serve their nations? This is not merely an administrative question. It is fundamentally a political one. Merit-based institutions require transparency, an inclusive political environment, an empowered civil society, freedom of expression, and access to information. Citizens must have confidence that professional competence and public integrity rather than political, familial, or personal proximity offer a genuine path into public service. Civil society should therefore not be treated merely as a beneficiary of the transition, nor consulted merely after major decisions are taken. It should be recognized as a partner in governance, oversight, and institution building. The third duality is between economic recovery and conditions necessary to make the recovery sustainable and credible. There is no serious path towards stability in Syria without economic recovery. Millions of Syrians require employment, infrastructure requires rehabilitation and investment, Syrian businesses need access to international financial markets and normalized banking relationships. The international community has an important responsibility here, and commitment to formal sanction relief alone is not enough. Overcompliance by private institutions continues to create economic barriers, even for lawful transactions. Governments lifting sanctions should therefore provide clear guidance to financial private institutions to facilitate legitimate economic engagement with Syria. But responsibility runs in both directions. Syria cannot ask international investors to accept risks and uncertainty that Syrians themselves would not accept. As economic reintegration progresses, the responsibility of Syrian authorities to provide clarity, predictability, and transparency also increases. Syria needs a clearer economic vision. What role will the private sector play? How will public assets be managed? What rules will govern foreign investments? And how will economic justice be upheld? Public procurement deserves particular attention. Government contracts and infrastructure projects should increasingly be governed by transparent procedures, competitive tenders, and meaningful mechanisms of oversight and appeal. These are not conditions imposed from abroad. These are safeguards for Syrian public funds and protections for Syrian citizens. Mr. President, across these three dualities, there is one common principle. The answer is not choosing one side and rejecting the other. Syria should not choose between sovereignty and cooperation. It should pursue sovereign cooperation. It should not choose between trust and qualification. It should build institutions in which credible qualifications earns trust. And it should not choose between rapid economic recovery and transparency. Transparency is precisely what will make economic recovery just and durable. I therefore conclude with the following concrete appeals. To the Syrian authorities, protect national ownership while facilitating access to international expertise, establish merit-based and transparent pathways into public service, guarantee meaningful space for civil society and fundamental freedoms, articulate a clear economic strategy, and strengthen transparent procurement and accountability mechanisms. To the international community, Consider convening a dedicated international donors conference for the rebuilding of Syria. Provide technical assistance centered on knowledge transfer and national capacity building. Support Syrian-led justice and institutional reform. Address banking overcompliance and mobilize responsible investment and development support. And to both sides, I would suggest one final principle: Do not measure success by how much authority is retained by the state, nor by how much assistance is delivered by the international community. Measure it by how much capability, accountability, and opportunity are ultimately transferred to the Syrian people. This is where sovereignty requires meeting. This is where national ownership becomes concrete. And this is where Syria's transition becomes one not merely diverging from the nation's past, but leading towards a functioning, inclusive, and prosperous state. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank Mr. Tabbara for his briefing. I now give-- we would like to thank the briefers for that. I now give the floor to those council members who wish to make statements. I give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

And I also thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone, Under-Secretary-General Fletcher, and Mr. Tabbara for their briefings. Mr. President, with High-Level Week approaching, we recall President al-Shara's address to the General Assembly last year, in which he spoke of a new chapter of peace, prosperity, and development for Syria. One year later, Syria has made remarkable progress in rebuilding institutions, and laying the foundations for economic recovery and a peaceful, prosperous future. Foreign Minister Leger Rasmussen saw this firsthand when he two weeks ago visited Syria and reopened the Danish Embassy in Damascus. However, emerging from the devastation of civil war, widespread atrocity crimes, and decades of oppression is not without challenges, and much remains to be done. At the outset, We reiterate Denmark's full support for Syria's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. We call on Israel to withdraw from Syrian territory and to comply fully with its obligations under the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement. The continued Israeli presence in southern Syria poses an increased risk of regional destabilization. We reaffirm our support for a diplomatic solution to address the security of southern Syria and express our concern about reports that the Syrian-Israeli talks have stalled. At this fragile time for the region, we call for their swift resumption. Mr. President, despite these serious security challenges, the political transition continues to take shape. To ensure a lasting peace, the political transition must follow international standards, a clear and transparent roadmap, and sound institutional checks and balances. The full participation of women, minorities, youth, and civil society in general remains essential. We welcome initiatives such as the Women's Police Academy and encourage continued security sector reform to build public trust. We also welcome the IAEA's historic and unanimous decision after 15 years to close the file on the previous regime's nuclear noncompliance now that Syria's nuclear material and facilities are under safeguards. We commend Syria for this achievement and encourage Syria to continue its cooperation with the IAEA, including through bringing into force an Additional Protocol. This complements the progress Syria has made in addressing outstanding issues related to the former regime's chemical weapons programme and the Syrian collaboration with the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Mr. President, we have also followed the important trials of senior former regime figures. Accountability of crimes committed against the Syrian people is essential, and all proceedings must be transparent, allow for appeal, and meet international fair trial standards. Transitional justice has to be impartial and respect the rights of all victims and survivors. Finally, Mr. President, the humanitarian situation remains alarming, with more than 15 million Syrians in need of assistance. Access remains limited to healthcare, food, clean water, education, and livelihoods, and as we've heard, rising fuel prices only exacerbates these problems. As we also have heard, there is a need to scale up funding not just for the humanitarian response, but also for recovery and reconstruction in order to ensure investments in recovery and in giving the Syrian people the future they aspire to and deserve. This is also why the Danish Foreign Minister, during his visit to Damascus last month, in addition to a large-scale humanitarian support, pledged 76 US dollars in ODA to Syria, millions of US dollars already donated to Syria, and stressed that Denmark plans to increase our support to reconstruction from 2027. In closing, Denmark will continue to support Syria, including through this Council, as it writes this new, brighter chapter of its history. I thank.

You. I.
Thank the representative of Denmark for her statement, and I give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

Mr. President, We are grateful to the Deputy Special Envoy, the Secretary General for Syria, Mr. Claudio Cordone, and to Mr. Tom Fletcher for their briefings, and we carefully listened to the representative of civil society. Our country has a keen interest in the swift stabilization of the military, political, and humanitarian situation in the Syrian Arab Republic. We note that there are both positive signs and also some serious challenges in terms of normalizing the situation in Syria. We support Damascus's consistent steps to unify the country and also we welcome the new authorities resolve to ensure the rights of all citizens irrespective of their ethnic or religious background as the state is being built the all representatives of Syrian society's interests need to be taken into consideration. Otherwise, any models for the future political structure will not be either sustainable nor viable. In this context, we are pleased to note the progress in achieving the January agreements on reintegrating the area beyond the Euphrates into the legal sphere of Syrian statehood. We hope that the comprehensive implementation of these understandings will help to achieve long-term normalisation of the situation in the north-east of the country. We view the launch of the work of the Syrian People's Assembly as an important step in the context of the Syrian authorities' work to shore up internal stability and national unity. We wish every success to parliamentarians who bear the important and also complex responsibility of hammering out a new constitution and other fundamental legislative acts. Regarding the socio-economic situation in Syria, there are worrisome reports of large-scale protests breaking out because of the worsening fuel crisis. Syrians' needs remain enormous. Two-thirds of the population of the country require humanitarian assistance. Nonetheless, we note the positive changes in the Syrian economy, primarily in agriculture. This year, wheat production may reach 2.7 million tons. This is particularly important because of volatility on the global food markets. in particular because of the reckless actions of Ukraine in the Black Sea waters and also the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. This month, more than 5 million Syrian children went to school. However, Syria's education system continues to encounter serious problems. An additional burden is being placed on the weakened infrastructure by the mass return of the population. In this regard, There is a real need to rebuild schools, the water supply and sanitation, and mines continue to be a serious threat. Explosive ordinances can be found in residential areas, including schools and playgrounds. Children account for about 30% of those killed and 40% of those injured as a result of explosions. There's a need to systematically inform the population of the dangers of mines. In 2025, Syria started to integrate relevant models into school curricula. We believe this work to be priority along with mine clearance and providing assistance to victims. All of these factors need to be taken into consideration when considering the current situation. However, solving these challenges really depends on having resources. The humanitarian response plan is only 30% We call for predictable financing of humanitarian operations in Syria in order to prevent a backsliding of these positive trends and in order to create conditions for a shift to sustainable development. So we're convinced that consolidating Syrian society and resolving its economic problems, curbing the risk of dividing the country and also combating terrorists, including FTFs, all these must remain top priorities. However, any discussions on stabilization in Syria lose all their meaning when at the same time steps are being taken from the outside which undermine the sovereignty of the country and its territorial integrity. We have consistently stood against the territory of the Syrian Arab Republic being used as an arena for geopolitical competition and settling of scores. We believe that the overarching responsibility of all constructive-minded states in the Middle East region and beyond to avoid steps that could cause another wave of escalation in the country. We would like to focus on the unacceptable nature of the aggressive actions by Israel against Syria, be this the occupation of a significant part of the country or ongoing IDF attacks and armed raids deep into its territory. We cannot fail to draw attention to the recent provocative visit of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Defence Minister Katz to the arbitrary IDF positions on Mount Hermon and also the statements of absolute control by Western Jerusalem of the area from Hermon to the Yarmouk River and also its ongoing expansionist ambitions in the region. Such actions and rhetoric not only run counter to international law, but also create the additional risk of region-wide instability, which is still experiencing the serious consequences of the American-Israeli military misadventures against Iran. We would urge Western Jerusalem to swiftly stop its arbitrary actions in the Syrian Golan and comply with the disengagement agreement and withdraw all Israeli troops from their positions. The legitimate concerns in the area of security cannot serve as justification for a violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Syria. The Israeli leadership needs to recognize that it is a dead end in nature to use military methods to eradicate problems. And it needs to listen to the common sense voices coming from Damascus that they're ready to negotiate. We're convinced that it is the political diplomatic path with a strict compliance with the norms of international law that can ensure long-term security for all Middle East region states. Russia, from its side, will continue to assist stabilization of friendly by having an inclusive political process, strengthening statehood, unity, and territorial integrity as part of Security Council Resolution 2254. I thank.

You.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for his statement, and I give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to today's briefers. The United States welcomes the ongoing progress that the Syrian authorities continue to make on political, humanitarian, and security priorities. As we noted last month, the United States, under President Trump, is committed to supporting a stable, unified Syria and to building a more prosperous and interconnected region. We welcome the IAEA Board's decision on September 9th to end its longstanding noncompliance finding for Syria. It reflects the government's commitment to cooperate, to cooperative engagement with the IAEA and to transparency about the former regime's clandestine nuclear program and to the peaceful use of nuclear technology going forward. We encourage Syria to continue working with the IAEA to strengthen its domestic safeguards of nuclear material, including by adopting an additional protocol and implementing its provisions in full. The conclusion of an additional protocol would be an important demonstration of the Syrian government's commitment to transparency and to fostering international trust. We also take this opportunity to remind Security Council members that 15 years ago, on June 2011, the Council first received notice from the IAEA that the Assad regime had violated its safeguards agreement. As we said at the time, it was obvious that Assad had tried to build a nuclear reactor in order to produce weapons-grade plutonium. And yet some members of this Council shamelessly parroted the Assad regime's lies and tried to deflect blame onto Israel. Colleagues, we now know that all along, the IAEA was right. Israel was right. The United States was right. We point this out not to boast, but to remind fellow council members and proliferator states like Iran that with enough time and effort, the truth will always prevail. As we did last month, the United States commends the Syrian Democratic Forces' integration into Syrian state institutions, marking further progress towards Syria's path to one army, one government, and one unified state. We remain concerned, however, by the escalation in Souweida, and reaffirm our support for the trilateral roadmap announced nearly a year ago by the United States, Syria, and Jordan, a path toward the dignified reintegration of the province and full rights and obligations of citizenship for its Druze community. We urge all parties to exercise restraint and pursue dialogue in earnest. And we look for continued progress toward accountability, security, and the safe return of the displaced. We also call on both Israel and Syria to exercise restraint and seek de-escalation in regard to territorial issues. The United States will continue to engage closely with both countries and with all regional stakeholders to promote dialogue and peaceful solutions. As we look ahead to UNGA High-Level Week next week, We encourage members of this Council and all Member States to use this opportunity for meaningful engagement with the Syrian Government in support of a stable, secure, and prosperous Syria, which, of course, is in the interest of the entire globe. We reiterate our call for UN institutions and Member States to support the Syrian Government's efforts to advance these goals. We urge the Syrian Government to work with the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism, the IIIM, and the Independent Institution on Missing Persons in Syria, the IIMP, to finalize MOUs that will enable them to provide resources to support the ongoing transitional justice project in Syria. We also take note of the Special Envoys and of the Under-Secretary-General, of their remarks regarding the role of women in Syria. Their ideas, their work, and insight of women is key to the stability and legitimacy of the new Syria. Their role in every sector is important and is clear in the search for the missing. Their vital role must be fostered in every dynamic. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of the United States for the statement, and I give the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, President, and I thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone, Under-Secretary-General Fletcher, and Mr. Tabbara for their briefings. President, last week marked a significant step forward in Syria's compliance with its international obligations, with the IAEA closure of Syria's long-standing safeguards file by consensus. After 15 years of obstruction by the Assad regime, this decision is an important symbol of Syria's commitment to meeting its international obligations. And we also commend Syria's constructive engagement with the OPCW. The United Kingdom stands ready to support the complete and verified destruction of Assad-era chemical weapons and the full implementation of Syria's obligations under the Chemical Weapons Convention. Lasting stability will not be delivered, though, by security arrangements alone. It must be underpinned by reconciliation, accountability and protection for all communities. We remain concerned by reports of ongoing violence in northeast Syria, and we continue to support a unified and inclusive Syria and encourage all parties to exercise restraint avoid inflammatory rhetoric and work together to resolve outstanding issues related to the implementation of the integration agreement. Ultimately, ensuring that all Syrians feel secure, represented and protected are an essential part of Syria's journey towards long-term stability and recovery. To support the recovery plans of the Syrian Government and the needs of the displaced and vulnerable populations, the United Kingdom will contribute $90 million this year. President, Syria's recovery remains fragile. Israel's actions risk increasing tensions at an already sensitive moment, including Prime Minister Netanyahu's recent visit to the summit of Mount Hermon in the UN area of separation. We continue to urge all parties to exercise restraint and avoid actions that could lead to further escalation, and call on Israel to set out a timeline for withdrawal from recently occupied Syrian territory. Dialogue remains the only sustainable path forwards. We encourage continued engagement between Syria and Israel, and welcome efforts to resolve differences through negotiation rather than confrontation. Respect for Syria's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence remains essential to securing long-term stability. The United Kingdom remains committed to supporting efforts to ensure that Syria emerges from decades of conflict as a stable, sovereign and inclusive state.
I thank the representative of the United Kingdom for the statement, and I give the floor to the representative of China.

Thank you, President. I thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone and Under-Secretary-General Fletcher for their briefings. I have also listened attentively to the statement made by civil society representative, Mr. Tabbara. While the situation in Syria is generally stabilizing, the country faces multiple daunting challenges, including intertwined internal and external security risks and the uphill struggle uphill struggle to improve people's lives, the Syrian transitional government should work in concert with the international community and adopt more practical measures in order to consolidate the hard-won positive momentum, effectively enhance the well-being of its people, and promote long-term stability and security across the country. I would like to make five points. First, Syria has largely completed the integration in its northeastern region and achieved significant additional progress in the political transition process. The transitional government has made positive efforts in this regard, which deserve recognition. China supports Syria as it continues to be guided by the spirit of Resolution 2254 and the principle of a Syrian-led and owned process, advances its domestic political process, and actively explores the Accords with its national conditions. Second, recent clashes and protests in certain Druze and Kurdish communities warrant the attention of all parties. The ability to effectively handle communal relations represents a test of the governance capacity of the transitional government. We hope that the Syrian transitional government will proceed from the interests of the entire Syrian population, heed the demands of various groups, protect the rights of all communities on an equal basis, resolve internal differences through inclusive dialogue, and promote national reconciliation and consensus-building. Third, a large number of foreign terrorist fighters remain active in Syria, posing a persistent threat and a grave risk to the country's peaceful reconstruction. Syria must never become a safe haven for terrorism. This is the consensus of the international community. China urges the Syrian transitional government to remain steadfast in its determination to counter terrorism and take all possible measures to effectively and resolutely combat all international terrorist organizations designated by the Council, including the ETIM. Fourth, conflict and upheaval are not Syria's destiny. The Syrian people deserve a new life in an environment of peace and stability. At present, Syria faces acute challenges regarding unemployment, inflation, and infrastructure. China supports the Syrian transitional government in making development and reconstruction its central task, and encourages Syria to foster a safe and welcoming business environment and create favorable conditions for economic recovery. We also call on the international community to sustain its humanitarian assistance to Syria and address the most pressing humanitarian needs. Fifth, the Golan Heights is occupied Syrian territory. The Security Council has adopted multiple resolutions demanding the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Syrian Golan. China respects Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity. We oppose the changing of the status quo through unilateral actions. China calls on Israel to cease all military operations in Syrian territory and withdraw its forces without delay. The 1974 Separation of Forces Agreement should be effectively observed. China supports the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force in carrying out its duty as mandated by the Council and without obstruction. President, next Monday marks the International Day of Peace. This day embodies the international community's aspiration to end all conflicts, as well as the shared vision of people across the globe for lasting peace. Restoring peace and stability to Syria and the wider Middle East region is an integral part of the global cause of peace and development. As a sincere friend to Syria and the countries of the Middle East, China will continue to play a constructive role in helping the country and the region achieve security, stability, and development at an early date. Thank you, President.
I thank the representative of China for the statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Colombia.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd like to thank the Deputy Special Envoy, Cordone, the Under-Secretary-General, Mr. Fletcher, and particularly Mr. Tabbara for his briefing. They've all shared much information with us and given us new avenues for discussion on this. I also welcome here the delegations joining us today. Mr. President, the political and humanitarian dimensions of the decisions taken in this body on Syria are based on a framework of concrete obligations. on the one hand, an inclusive political process, and on the other, safe, sustained and unhindered access across the country's territory, as well as addressing the humanitarian crisis. This framework was designed to manage an open conflict and today to supporting a transition. And it is during the transition where it will be possible to verify compliance with these obligations. Colombia welcomes the achievements of the transitional government, the integration of the northeast, the inauguration of the People's Assembly on 12 July, the designation of the Constitutional Court and the recognition of the civic and cultural rights of Syrian Kurds. These are all steps towards the inclusive processes that this Council requested. On the humanitarian pillar, the return of more than 3 million persons is the most eloquent indicator, perhaps, of the restored trust, depending as it does on sustained assistance. In the humanitarian sphere, the funding gap isn't an abstract figure. It has direct verifiable consequences. The fall in emergency food assistance mentioned by USG Fletcher of 1.3 million from 1.3 million people to 650,000 shows that resource shortfalls immediately translate into deprivation. Colombia calls on donors to boost the funding of the response plan. Finally, but no less importantly, the explosive remains of war are today one of the main obstacles to sustainable return. They have claimed more than 2,000 victims since December 2024, one every six hours. More than 60% of the incidents happen in agricultural and agricultural land or grazing land, meaning that contamination threatens life, food and return all at the same time. Colombia calls for increased funding and humanitarian demining capacities, as well as risk education. We also call for comprehensive assistance to victims to be incorporated in the recovery agenda from the outset. The progress achieved shows that the framework created by this Council can produce verifiable results. Completing it now demands more than political support. It means ensuring that the recovery is funded. The World Bank estimates the recovery needs at $216 billion. The UNDP has calculated that at the current rate, it will take Syria 55 years to recover its pre-conflict level of output, and 15 years at a growth rate of 5%. Although the lifting of sanctions designations has, however, opened space for investment that didn't exist two years ago. President, living up to these standards is what will turn the efforts of the transition into lasting results. Colombia will continue to support an inclusive, Syrian-led, UN-facilitated process. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Colombia for that statement. I give the floor to the representative of Bahrain.

Thank you, Madam President. We would like to express our thanks to Mr. Claudio Cordani, Deputy Special Envoy of the Secretary General of the United Nations for Syria, and Mr. Tom Fletcher, Under-Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator in the Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the OCHA, for their comprehensive briefings on the latest developments in Syria. We have taken note of the intervention by the civil society representative, Mr. Yasser Tabbara. I would also to welcome the participation of the Permanent Representatives in today's session. Mr. President, the Syrian Arab Republic today stands at a pivotal stage in its efforts to restore security and stability and to build national and constitutional institutions capable of meeting the aspirations of the Syrian people for peace, security, and development. The Kingdom of Bahrain believes that the success of this stage requires continued support for the efforts of the Syrian government aimed at strengthening the rule of law, promoting social peace and national reconciliation, and fostering the values of tolerance and peaceful coexistence in a manner that strengthens the unity of the social fabric and ensures the participation of all segments of the Syrian people in the building of their future. In the context of supporting Syria's return to the paths of cooperation and active engagement with international institutions, we welcome the adoption by the IAEA Board of Governors of the resolution concerning the Syrian Arab Republic and the resulting conclusion of consideration of the agenda item on the implementation of the Safeguards Agreement in Syria. We hope that this will constitute a further step towards strengthening confidence and cooperation between Syria and international institutions, opening broader avenues to support its stability and recovery. Bahrain commends the efforts of the Arab Group on the IAEA Board of Governors, chaired by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with the participation of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, the Arab Republic of Egypt and the Kingdom of Morocco, and its role in submitting the draft resolution. The achievement of sustainable stability in Syria remains linked, first and foremost, to the full respect of its sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity. Thus, the Kingdom of Bahrain expresses its rejection of the continued Israeli attacks and incursions into Syrian territory, including the recent developments in southern Syria and the Golan Heights, and stresses the need to refrain from any measures or practices that would seek to create a new reality on the ground or undermine and the sovereignty, unity, and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic. In a related context, the Kingdom of Bahrain encourages diplomatic effort aimed at de-escalation and strengthening security and stability, as well as the continued dialogue in a manner that contributes to reaching understandings that safeguard the security and stability of the region based on a full respect for the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic. This is in accordance with international law and relevant UN resolutions. In this regard, the Kingdom stresses the need to comply with the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, including Resolution 497, and to halt escalation and refrain from anything that could undermine security and stability in Syria and the region. The Kingdom also reaffirms the importance of the role played by the UN Disengagement Observer Force, UNDOF, and the need to ensure the safety of its personnel, their freedom of movement, and their ability to fully implement its mandate. Mr. President, on the humanitarian front, the return of increasing number of Syrians to their country constitute an encouraging development. However, the sustainability of such returns requires providing them with the conditions of a dignified life, restoring basic services, creating livelihood opportunities, and rehabilitating damaged infrastructure. Against this backdrop, the Kingdom of Bahrain calls upon the international community and donor community to continue supporting the humanitarian response and to ensure unhindered access to assistance for all those in need, while simultaneously expanding early recovery and reconstruction programs, thereby creating the conditions conducive to the voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return of refugees and IDPs. In conclusion, we renew our solidarity with the brotherly Syrian Arab Republic and support for all efforts aimed at strengthening its security, stability, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. The Kingdom of Bahrain looks forward to the international community's continuing to work alongside the Syrian people to build a future characterized by security, peace, development, and prosperity. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Bahrain for that statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Somalia.

Madam President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the A3, namely the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Liberia, and my own country, Somalia. We thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone and Under-Secretary-General Fletcher for their comprehensive briefings. We thank Mr. Tabbara for his contribution and welcome the participation of the Permanent Representative of the Syrian Arab Republic in this meeting. The A3 welcomes the positive momentum in Syria, despite persistent challenges The Syrian government has shown resolve in restoring national institutions, consolidating stability, promoting national unity, and responding to the aspirations of its people. In this regard, we wish to make the following points. First, we acknowledge the Syrian Government's steps toward national integration and institutional consolidation, including the decision of August 25th concerning the dissolution and the integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces into the national defense architecture. This is a significant step toward unified security structures and a stronger state authority. We encourage continued progress on inclusive governance, the participation of women and youth, representation of all communities, and human rights. We reaffirm that Security Council Resolution 2254 remains the central framework for a Syrian-led and a Syrian-owned political process. Second. We recognize the government's cooperation with the United Nations and humanitarian partners to facilitate assistance, restore services, and support the return of Syrians. The return of more than 3.5 million displaced persons and refugees signal renewed confidence. Yet millions still require lifesaving aid, while funding shortfalls threaten essential operations. Sustainable returns require security, housing, schools, healthcare, and public services. We call for predictable funding for humanitarian assistance, as well as early recovery activities. Third, economic recovery is essential to sustainable peace. We welcome Syria's removal from the United States State Sponsors of Terrorism list on August 24th. This important step can support financial reintegration, trade, investment, and public service delivery. Syrian government is working under challenging conditions to stabilize the economy and rehabilitate infrastructure. Rising fuel and commodity prices continue to strain households. We call for constructive economic engagement and unhindered investment to restore utilities, protect vulnerable communities, and create sustainable livelihoods. Fourth, we deplore continued military strikes and ground incursions inside Syria, which threaten civilians, undermine stabilization, and risk regional escalation. We take serious note of the International Independent Commission of Inquiry's finding of 8 September concerning the unlawful incursions, arbitrary raids, and expanding buffer zones in southern Syria. We call for the release of detained Syrian nationals and an end to unilateral cross-border operations. The occupied Syrian Golan remains an integral part of Syria under Resolution 497 of 1981. The 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement must be fully respected. The clashes in Al-Suwayda underscore the need for de-escalation, local dialogue, reconciliation, and national cohesion. We support the government's efforts to restore calm and address local grievances through inclusive engagement. We also commend the Syrian authorities for confronting ISIL-Daesh and other violent extremist groups. Unified national security mechanisms and coordinated international partnership consistent with international law, remain vital to preventing their resurgence. To conclude, Madam President, the A3 reaffirms its unwavering commitment to Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity. We recognize the government's positive steps to consolidate institutions advance integration and improve security, as well as establishing the foundation for economic recovery. We urge the Security Council and the wider international community to work constructively with the Syrian Government and support the Syrian people in their pursuit of national reconciliation, recovery, stability and lasting peace. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Somalia and I give the floor to the representative of Greece.

Thank you, Madam President, and I thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone, USG Fletcher, as well as Mr. Tabbara for their valuable contributions. Madam President, Syria is at the moment of profound transition. There is now a real opportunity to move from a country emerging from conflict to a country rebuilding its institutions and fully reclaiming its place in the international community. I would like to make three points. First, institutions must now deliver on the promise of an inclusive transition. The establishment and convening of the People's Assembly, as well as the announcement of the composition of its committees, are important milestones. But representation must be more than a formal exercise. Women and all components of Syrian society, regardless of their ethnic or religious background, must have a meaningful voice in shaping the country's future. The next major test will be the constitutional project, one that protects rights and guarantees equality before the law for all Syrian citizens. The same principle applies to transitional justice. There can be no lasting reconciliation without accountability and no accountability without equal protection for all victims. The adoption of the General Assembly resolution on women searchers of missing persons last week, which Greece was proud to co-sponsor, is a reminder that the fate of those who remain missing continues to be one of the deepest wounds of the conflict. We welcome the steps taken to address the trauma of the conflict and the increasing engagement of the Syrian authorities with international mechanisms. We encourage further engagement with the IIIM and all relevant institutions. Second, Syria's opening to the international community must now translate into recovery and opportunity. The real test will be whether a new economic horizon translates into a better life for ordinary Syrians. Recovery must reach communities across the country and give young Syrians a reason to build their future at home. At the same time, humanitarian assistance remains necessary. Greece will be at Syria's side during this transition. It stands ready to contribute to Syria's recovery and to efforts that strengthen its links with the wider international community. Third, Syria's political opening must be matched by a genuine security settlement. We welcome the completion of the process leading to the dissolution of the Syrian Democratic Forces and their integration into the Syrian state institutions. This is a significant step towards restoring the unity of the Syrian state and consolidating its sovereignty. At the same time, integration must be coupled with guarantees for the rights and meaningful participation of the Kurdish community in Syrian institutions. The situation in Suweida also requires sustained attention. It cannot be allowed to falter or disintegrate. The September 2025 roadmap must be fully implemented, while the restoration of trust between communities and state institutions must remain at the core of all efforts, with the aim of a truly inclusive Syria. The same is true for Syria's relations with its neighbors. We encourage direct contacts between Syria and Israel, facilitated by the United States. De-escalation must remain the immediate priority, while negotiations should contribute to durable security arrangements. Greece reiterates its firm respect for Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity. All violations must therefore cease, and the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement must be respected. In conclusion, Madam President, Syria's transition must belong to Syrians, all Syrians. The international community now has a responsibility to help make that transition work. Syria has come a long way in a short period of time. The task now is to make this progress irreversible. Greece will continue to support a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned transition. an inclusive political process, accountability and reconciliation, economic recovery, and a Syria that is sovereign, united, stable, and at peace with itself and its neighbours. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Greece, and I give the floor to the representative of Latvia.

Thank you, Madam President.

I thank the Deputy Special Envoy for Syria, Claudio Cordone, and Under-Secretary-General Tom Fletcher for their informative briefings, as well as Mr. Yasser Tabbara for his contribution. Madam President, following decades of devastating civil war and dictatorship, and amidst the ongoing turbulence in the wider Middle East, Syria strives for stability, both internally and at its borders. Stability is essential for advancing Syria's political transition and reconstruction. Over the past year and a half, Syria's new government has achieved substantial progress. The resilience of the Syrian people and their desire for a dignified life are at the heart of this process. We recognize the principles of transparency, cooperation, and responsibility demonstrated by the Syrian Government. as it restores the country's place in the international political and economic arena. We encourage for the same principles to be prioritized in further strengthening Syria's social cohesion. Transparency regarding decisions taken, continuous engagement with a free and open Syrian civil society, Meaningful participation of women in political decision-making and inclusive representation of all ethnic and religious communities and political processes are essential to ensuring broad and genuine Syrian ownership of the transition. We look forward to the significant legislative work to be undertaken by the People's Assembly, including the drafting of the permanent constitution. The Syrian people rightfully await the restoration of the rights and freedoms of which they were deprived for the last six decades. People's expectation of being represented and heard particularly underscores the deeply symbolic role embodied by the new parliament. We also underscore the importance of conditions conducive for continuation of dignified return of refugees and internally displaced persons, including through mine action and reducing risks and ensuring safety of affected communities. And we echo USG Fletcher's assessment that there is a genuine potential for Syria to move towards recovery while acknowledging that humanitarian needs remain significant. And Syrian population continues to face economic hardship exacerbated by growing fuel prices. So it is clear that full social economic recovery will require continued efforts, time, investments, and sustained international solidarity. Madam President, rebuilding the rule of law and restoring confidence in public institutions, recognizing the suffering of victims and providing answers to families of missing persons are essential steps towards healing the painful scars of the past and contributing to lasting peace in Syria. Beyond ensuring accountability for the crimes of the former regime and preventing their occurrence, the Syrian people look forward to a genuinely comprehensive and transparent transitional justice process. And we commend the results achieved through the IIIM and call for the Syrian government and the relevant national bodies to continue their constructive engagement with international mechanisms and organizations and further facilitate their work on the ground. We welcome and encourage further contributions from countries to support Syrian law enforcement agencies, investigative authorities, prosecutorial authorities, and judges. We also acknowledge the commitment by the new Syrian government to resolve questions inherited from the ousted Assad regime that is well reflected by the ongoing work on the elimination of chemical weapons program and recently on the declared nuclear materials. And we commend the cooperation between the Syrian authorities and the IAEA that has led to a decision taken by Board of Governors to close the outstanding issues related to Syria's nuclear file. Turning to the external dimension, Syria's demonstrated commitment to fostering regional stability has opened up new opportunities for the normalization of relations with its neighbors as well as for integration into regional economic corridors and attraction of international investment. And we welcome this trajectory and encourage Syria to build on these positive developments, further strengthening its role as a constructive and responsible regional partner. Even though this Council, in its resolution 2824, has unanimously underscored that there should be no military activity of any kind in the area of separation, military actions in the Syrian Golan continue. They violate relevant UN resolutions and the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and are by no means a sustainable solution to Israel's security concerns either. We encourage Israel and Syria to resume negotiations towards mutually acceptable security arrangements in full compliance with international law and respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic and ensuring the protection of civilians on both sides of the border. In conclusion, We call on the international community to remain steadfast in its support for Syria as it advances along the path of political transition, recovery and reconstruction. And the United Nations is uniquely placed to support Syria-led priorities by bringing together its political, humanitarian, development and institution-building capacities. Latvia continues to support the people of Syria in their efforts towards a stable, peaceful and prosperous future. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia, and I give the floor to the representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Madam President. We thank Deputy Special Envoy Cordone, USG Fletcher, and Mr. Tabbara for their briefings. President, Syria has traveled a considerable distance in a remarkably short period. What began as a moment of profound transition is increasingly becoming a process of national consolidation, rebuilding state institutions, restoring Syria's unity, reconnecting with the region and the wider international community, and laying the foundations for recovery after years of devastating conflict. We appreciate the determined efforts of the Syrian Government in steering the country through this consequential period. We welcome the continued efforts towards the unification and consolidation of the Syrian state. Progress in the implementation of arrangements concerning the northeast Including the integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces and other institutions into the structures of the state represent an important step towards restoring Syria's unity. We encourage all concerned to continue addressing outstanding matters through dialogue, accommodation, and mutual understanding. A process that brings all Syrians together and strengthens national institutions will provide the strongest foundation for Syria's future. We equally recognize the considerable efforts being undertaken to restore governance, security, and normalcy across the country, despite immense challenges. The fight against terrorism remains critical. The terrorist groups, including foreign terrorist fighters, continue to pose a threat. Syria should receive the international cooperation and capacity-building support necessary to confront terrorism effectively in accordance with international law. President, Syria continues to bear the enormous economic, humanitarian, and infrastructural consequences of years of conflict. In this context, the lifting of sanctions by the United States and the European Union represents an important step forward. The growing investment and economic engagement of partners and brotherly countries, including from the Gulf region and the European Union, will contribute meaningfully to restoring livelihoods and creating the foundations for development. At this critical juncture, Syria's transition must not be undermined by external actions. Israel's continued military activities and presence on Syrian territory constitute violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity must be fully respected. along with strict observance of the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions. We strongly condemn the recent incursions into Syrian territory by senior Israeli officials, including at Mount Hermon, which constitute a flagrant violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Israel must vacate Syrian Golan and other occupied territory in Syria. Mr. President, the Syrian people have endured extraordinary suffering. Today, however, there is also a genuine opportunity before them. The task now is to consolidate these gains. Pakistan will continue to stand with the Syrian people and support a Syrian-led and Syrian-owned process that leads towards a peaceful, united, sovereign, and prosperous Syria. I thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Pakistan for that statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Thank you, President. We are grateful for the briefings of the Deputy Special Envoy for Syria, Mr. Claudio Cordone, the Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, Mr. Tom Fletcher, and of Yasser Tabbara, the co-founder of Syrian Forum. In addition, we recognize here the presence of the representatives of the Syrian Arab Republic, Israel, Turkey and Oman, who honor us with their participation today. Panama is diligently following the development of the situation in Syria and the positive ongoing efforts made by Syria to consolidate an inclusive political transition, to address the population's humanitarian needs and to move forward towards economic recovery. We believe that these three elements are closely interlinked and stand as complementary dimensions of one same objective. laying the foundations for a stable, sovereign, peaceful Syria. Consolidating this new phase also demands having a regional environment that allows Syria to focus its efforts on national reconstruction. In this context, we reiterate our steadfast commitment to Syria's sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity, and to the respect for its internationally recognized borders. We believe that it is essential for regional disputes to be addressed through diplomatic means and for all actors to refrain from action that might give rise to further trends of instability. President, millions of Syrians continue to be in need of humanitarian assistance, while the funding gap is increasingly hampering the response capacity. The fall in food aid observed by the World Food Programme and the shortages faced by multiple health facilities reveal how the lack of resources is having direct effects on people's lives. For this reason, we recognize the considerable efforts made by the United Nations, by humanitarian agencies and by their partners to continue providing assistance to millions of people. Against this backdrop, we reiterate our staunch support for the relocation of the Special Envoy's office to Damascus. Once there, we believe that it can continue to work to support the transition process more effectively. At the same time, we are encouraged by the progress made in terms of returns. More than 2 million IDPs and around 1.8 million refugees have returned to their place of origin. However, these returns in turn give rise to new needs, making it necessary to guarantee adequate, sustainable conditions so that people can rebuild their lives. We value the coordinated efforts being made to address the explosive remains of war to ensure that they do not continue to claim the lives of victims and restrict access to homes, farmlands, basic services and livelihoods. Furthermore, we are pleased to note the signs pointing to greater opening of the Syrian economy and a gradual reintegration into the international financial system. Sanctions relief and the timely decision by the United States to withdraw Syria from the list of states co-sponsors of terrorism warrant our recognition, since they have contributed to creating an environment conducive to investment and trade. Furthermore, we note with interest the increasing commitment from the private sector and countries in the region to Syria's recovery. These initiatives can contribute to restoring the country's productive capacity, creating jobs and strengthening livelihoods. However, these new opportunities must go hand in hand with a response that is in line with the scale of the persistent challenges. In this context, the recent difficulties related to the rise in global fuel prices highlight the need for this progress to translate into concrete improvements in people's daily lives. President, the resilience shown by the Syrian people and their hope for a better future deserve to be honored through an economic recovery rebuilding not only the country but also the lives of those living there. Panama will continue supporting the efforts of the United Nations, the international community and Syrian authorities to build a sovereign, prosperous and peaceful Syria that offers a better future to its entire population. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Panama for that statement, and I shall now make a statement in my capacity as representative of France.

First and foremost, I'd like to thank the Director's Special Envoy, Mr. Claudio Codona, and Under-Secretary-General for Humanitarian Affairs, Tom Fletcher, and Mr. Yasser Tabbara, representative of civil society, and I welcome the representatives of the Syrian Arab Republic, Turkey, Israel, and Oman. Since our last meeting, the Syrian transition has remained on a positive trajectory, even if it remains fragile. I'd like to focus on recent developments in my comments. I'd like to underscore the importance of the commitments upheld by Damascus before highlighting the challenges still facing it. Firstly, Syria continues to show its determination to reintegrate into the international community fully. The Board of Governors of the IAEA adopted a consensus resolution triggering the formal closure of the Syrian nuclear dossier, 15 years after it noted systemic violations by the Bashar al-Assad regime of its obligations. We have the proof, thanks to the in-depth investigations of the IAEA that the regime was conducting an illegal military program and undermined the non-proliferation architecture. In a spirit of transparency and responsibility, the new Syrian authorities have reported on secret sites, thus demonstrating their desire to eliminate this program once and for all. This decision by the Board of Governors of the IAEA rewards the speeding up of cooperation between Damascus and the IAEA. It reflects the work conducted by the OPCW on the elimination of chemical weapons, also inherited from the Assad regime. This is a rare advance in a landscape that has been degraded by non-proliferation issues.
