In the area of transitional justice, the technical cooperation framework between the Syrian authorities and the IIIM on Syria will facilitate the accomplishment of this mission to build a just and lasting peace. The work underway on a transitional justice law is part of this same goal. Furthermore, the integration of the Syrian Democratic Forces into the state is a historic step forward towards a sovereign, pluralistic Syria. The rights of all components of Syrian society, in particular the cultural and linguistic rights of the Kurds, need to come to fruition. Secondly, the efforts to make progress in the political transition need to be highlighted, such as the establishment of the People's Assembly, the return of millions of IDPs and refugees. But these efforts have been undermined by internal and external threats. The respect for civilian sovereignty is not negotiable. The repeated incursions by Israel decided upon at the highest level, undermine stability in the region. France calls for an immediate cessation of Israeli incursions and the resumption of security discussions between Israel and Syria. The situation in the south of Syria remains unstable. France calls for the immediate implementation of the Syrian-Jordan-American roadmap on Soueida in the interests of the local population, in particular the Druze community that wants to live in peace. Thirdly, it is up to us, the international community, to assist efforts underway. The gradual lifting of sanctions and the implementation of a reliable banking framework will help to rebuild trust to attract investments. It is absolutely crucial that humanitarian assistance continue and a development program be launched whilst thousands and thousands of refugees are seeking to return home. We commemorated last week, the 25th anniversary of the tragedy of the 11th of September 2001 terrorist attacks, and so we would encourage Syria to continue its unfailing fight against Daesh. Let us reiterate our support to building a stable, sovereign and unified Syria. I work again as the President of the Council, and I'd like now to give the floor to the representative of the Syrian Arab Republic.

I thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I'd like to thank the briefers. Mr. Claudio, I thank him for his statement and his support for Syria, and welcome back from Syria. And as you've seen for yourself there, we also watched you from here over there, and we did that as we miss Damascus and Syria and all of its governorates. I thank Mr. Fletcher for the clarity in which he spoke on the challenges as well as the achievements that the Syrian Government has made and the international community's support. I also thank Mr. Yasser Tabbara for all that he's offered us before the liberation from the society and after liberation, and we are working extensively with civil society in the new Syria. I also thank you, all members of the Security Council, once again and repeatedly and always for your support to Syria collectively. Mr. President. As some members of the Council said this time last year, Syria was preparing for its first historic participation in the high-level week of the General Assembly back then. And as you may recall, Syria came to New York carrying its vision for engaging with the international family after decades, long decades of absence. We came to tell the world on what we intended to do. But this year, Syria comes having seized this opportunity and matched its words with actions. Syria has become an indispensable and inevitable partner in ensuring security and stability in the region. Mr. President, today I had hoped to tell you how we completed the building of state institutions. I had wanted to explain how we completed the process of military and administrative integration. I wanted to brief you on the major steps that we have taken in combating Daesh and terrorist organizations, to inform you of our efforts in dismantling drug trafficking networks. I had wanted to show you how we succeeded in building excellent relations with neighboring countries, and to share the details of the visit of a large American trade delegation, the first of its kind, that came to Damascus to visit us two days ago and to shed light on the results of the Syrian government's efforts that have led, as you have mentioned, to the return of millions of refugees and internally displaced persons and the return of the world to Syria. Unfortunately, Mr. President, I find myself compelled, particularly as Netanyahu's government has sent its representative to participate in today's Syria session, I am compelled to devote this statement to discussing the greatest threat facing the stability of the entire region, not just Syria. How could I not do that when the Security Council bears the primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security? How could I not when all of you witnessed two weeks ago the unlawful entry of Israeli occupation officials into Syria in a blatant violation that was not just rejected by Syria but was rejected by 45 four countries that have chosen in less than 24 hours to stand by Syria here outside this Council's chamber to affirm the necessity to respect international law and national sovereignty. Mr. President, we, and from the very first moment, have demonstrated the sincerity of our intentions and our actions, and so did Israel. Therefore, today I will present to you what they said and what we said, and what they did and what we did since then. They said and we said that establishing security is an indispensable necessity. Israel penetrated our villages, displaced our people, bombed our facilities. While we chose to spare the region further suffering, we chose to open the door to mediation. They said and we said that differences should be addressed through dialogue. However, they evaded their diplomatic obligations, and they responded to dialogue with airstrikes, incursions, and violations and attacks, while we engage in good faith with the American initiative that we appreciate. They said, and we said, that the era of development and prosperity for the region has come. But they ignited tensions and unrest. They killed Syrians. They openly boasted about occupying Syria and the unlawful entry of their officials for narrow electoral reasons. While Syria, in the meantime, became a bridge for development, prosperity, and energy transit among the countries of the region. Syria became a pillar of regional stability. They said, and we said, that acting responsibly and engaging with the international community is imperative. But they restricted the international organizations' work in Syria. They obstructed our efforts to address the legacy of the former regime on the chemical weapons and the nuclear materials and other issues, whereas Syria engaged with the United Nations, with the OPCW, with the International Atomic Energy Agency, and facilitated their work, as you have all commended, colleagues. mention all of this not for rhetorical effect and not for out of a desire for making comparisons but I do this to state things clearly yes we want to move towards diplomatic solutions and a security agreement under American sponsorship and with your support we have demonstrated this by action and not by deed and not just by word by opening the door to dialogue from the very first moment but this under no circumstances means that we accept occupation or relinquish the rights of our people In closing, Mr. President, let us together write a different chapter in our history, a chapter whose title is stability and development, not war and aggression. We would be fortunate if we were to seize this opportunity so that history would remember that we chose to build, not to destroy, to cooperate, not to fight, to establish prosperity and not suffering. Mr. President, our region has always been mentioned in the divine texts and in the texts of history. And today, we find ourselves before a golden opportunity so that history would write about us. So how do we wish history to remember us? I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of the Syrian Arab Republic for the statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Israel.

Thank you, Mr. President. It has been nearly two years since the fall of the Assad regime. Since then, Syria has changed. There is a new government. The international community has engaged with it. And we hear new voices from Damascus. We welcome these developments. We believe in a promising future for Syria, and we believe in a promising future between Israel and Syria. That is why Israel has engaged directly with the new Syrian government to reach a security agreement. Syria must control its own territory. If Syria wants to be a trusted member of the international community, it cannot allow its territory to become a platform for terrorists, foreign militaries, and regional instability. Mr. President, Assad's fall created a power vacuum in Syria, and that vacuum is being exploited. ISIS terrorists are escaping prisons and rebuilding their cells. Hezbollah is using Syrian territory as a smuggling route for Iranian weapons, and Iran's Quds Force threatens Israel directly from Syrian territory. Even the Syrian government understands these threats. In July, Syria announced that it caught a Hezbollah weapons shipment near the Syria-Iraq border. It was hidden inside an oil tanker truck. What was inside the oil tanker? Long-range weapons, guided anti-tank missiles, and drones. These were not defensive munitions. They were advanced weapons. These weapons were moving. through Syrian territory, toward the Mediterranean coast, and ultimately to the hands of Hezbollah in Lebanon to target us, to target Israelis. Unfortunately, the Syrian government is limited in its ability to block the wave of smuggling coming from Iran through its territory. Additionally, Syria continues to face serious internal instability. Just this week, we saw the largest protest in Syria since the fall of the Assad regime. Rising costs and worsening economic conditions are driving unrest throughout the country. These developments should concern all of us, because instability creates opportunities, opportunities for ISIS, opportunities for Iran, Hezbollah and Hamas, and opportunities for foreign powers seeking to expand their influence. Mr. President, we should be aware of the radical Islamist threat in the Middle East. We remember what happened when radical Islam dominated Syria. We remember the ISIS beheadings of American journalists and British aid workers, on Syrian soil. We in Israel, we saw even more horrifying quality on October 7th in Israel. Ambassador Olabi, to refresh your memory, you can turn on Netflix and watch Fauda and see the visuals of what happened on October 7th. Israel does not leave its security to chance. That is why Israel maintains a small security buffer in the Golan Heights as a defensive measure. It is designed to prevent an October 7th-style cross-border attack from Syrian territory. We are not speaking only about the threats from inside Syria. There are also external threats. This brings me to the real question before this Council today. If Israel's tiny defensive buffer is considered a threat to Syrian stability, then what about a foreign power that control a much larger portion of Syrian territory and is building its military presence there? I am talking about Turkey. Mr. President, for years, Turkey has presented itself as a stabilizing force in our region, a NATO member state, a country that can speak to adversaries, a self-proclaimed regional power that can maintain order. Today, Turkey claims to be a partner in Syria's reconstruction. They claim to rebuild Syria's airports, provide energy, help Syria address its housing shortage. Look at what is really happening in Syria. Turkey intends to expand its own military capabilities inside Syria and take over the country. Today, they have 20,000 troops and over 100 bases in Syria. Perhaps this behavior rings a bell. Turkey is following the Iranian proxy playbook. Look at what happened in Lebanon, we speak about it every month, which became a hotbed for Iranian-backed Hezbollah for decades. Look how hard it is for Lebanon to regain its independence after years of being controlled by Iranian terrorist proxies. So I ask, is this stabilization or is this expansion? Because there is a pattern here. Turkey has repeatedly expanded its military presence beyond its borders, including in Cyprus, Iraq, and Libya. This is not simply about helping a neighbor to rebuild. It is about deepening influence. It is about advancing military ambitions. And it is about taking over a neighboring country. Even President Erdogan's own words should make us pay attention. He said, in a quote, to create a country whose horizons cannot be confined. He meant what he said. Take a look at this map. Look at the tiny, tiny sliver of territory. This is the Israeli security buffer consisting 0.1% of Syria. Now, Look north. As of now, Turkey controls 5% of Syria. That is 50 times the size of Israel's security buffer. Yet somehow, Israel's tiny defensive buffer is presented as a threat to Syrian sovereignty. If we are serious about sovereignty, then we must apply the same standard and condemnations to everyone. Mr. President, this is where Turkey's presence becomes directly relevant to Israel. Turkey is not merely expanding its military footprint. Its leadership has adopted increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel. The Turkish foreign minister has called Israel, and I quote, "burden that humanity can no longer bear." We have also heard blatant anti-Semitism from President Erdogan. He will come here on Tuesday. We will listen to him in the General Assembly. I think he's the third or fourth speaker on the list. We know what he will say, because we heard him in the past. President Erdogan accused Israel of, and I quote, "feeding on the blood of innocents," and has repeatedly called for Israel's destruction. including to, quote, "destroy and devastate Zionist Israel." He equated Israeli leaders to the Nazis from the podium of the General Assembly. Erdogan's actions support his words. Erdogan proudly supports Hamas terrorists. Erdogan hosts Hamas and Hezbollah leaders and facilitates their banking infrastructure. Erdogan has turned Turkey into a Hamas base of operations. So when Turkey moves its military presence deeper into Syria, we have to ask a simple question: What are Turkey's real intentions? Mr. President, we know what genuine stabilization looks like. It means building a secure and prosperous future for the Syrian people. It does not mean building military footholds. It does not mean expanding foreign military influence and certainly does not mean allowing Syrian territory to become a platform for Turkish aggression against Israel. So I ask this Council, what would any nation do in this scenario? We learned on October 7th that when someone threatens Israel, we better believe them. Mr. President, The blame for this instability does not rest on Turkey alone. We heard the Syrian ambassador claim last week that sovereignty is not selective and territorial integrity is non-negotiable. Then apply those words to Turkey. He sits right next to you. When Israel is involved, you gather a press conference to condemn us, but when Turkey occupies Syrian territory, You remain silent. Your outrage is selective. Your silence is revealing. Ambassador Walabi, let's be honest. We both know the facts. We asked Syria to prevent Turkiye from taking over the Al-Dawal base within your territory. That was our red line. When Syria ignored the message, We sent it another way. If Syria is serious about re-entering the international community, it cannot allow itself to become a breeding ground for instability. We will not accept this, and the international community should not either. Let me be clear and conclude. We want to see a stable Syria. We want to see a sovereign Syria. and we want to see a Syria that controls its territory. But we will never accept a Syria whose territory is used to threaten Israel, not by Hezbollah or Hamas, not by ISIS, and not by Turkey. Thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you, representative of Israel, for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of Turkey.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I would like to thank USG Fletcher, Deputy Special Envoy Cordon, and Mr. Tabbara for their comprehensive briefings. Mr. President, Syria continues to advance towards stabilization despite challenges. Through its constructive engagement with the international community, including this Council, the Syrian Government continues to make meaningful progress in addressing the grave legacy of the former regime. In this regard, we commend Syria for its commitment to fulfilling its obligations under the Treaty of Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, its close cooperation with the IAEA, and the transparency it has demonstrated. Reflecting this constructive approach, the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a resolution by consensus on 9 September, closing Syria's nuclear non-compliance file and permanently removing the matter from its agenda. We welcome this resolution and congratulate the Syrian people and government. Mr. President, sustained international support for Syria remains essential to security and stability in the region and beyond. The announcement of the dissolution of the so-called SDF and the progress made in the integration process are particularly important developments. We will continue to follow the next steps. in collaboration with the Syrian Government and the international community. This process needs to be concluded in a manner that reinforces Syria's sovereignty, territorial integrity, unity and social cohesion. Mr. President, it remains essential to sustain reconstruction efforts and create the conditions necessary for the return of all Syrians who fled the atrocities of the former regime and Daesh. In this regard, we welcome the growing international economic engagement with the Syrian authorities. The international community should build on this positive momentum. Mr. President, regrettably, Israel continues to undermine this positive trajectory through its reckless attacks and statements against Syria. The illegal entry of high-level Israeli officials in the occupied Syrian territory is yet another example of Israel's provocative and destabilizing actions against Syria. We condemn Israel's relentless attacks, which target Syria's infrastructure and capabilities, and violate its sovereignty and territorial integrity. We reiterate our call on Israel to comply fully with the 1974 Disengagement of Force Agreement, refrain from further escalation, and reverse its encroachments on Syrian territory. The international community, and this Council in particular, must use all means at its disposal to bring an end to Israel's aggression against Syria and its occupation of Syrian territory. It is also concerning that illegal Druze armed groups, relying on Israeli support, continue their destabilizing activities in Syria, including by preventing students from sitting their examinations. and obstructing delivery of essential supplies to the governorate. Mr. President, at last month's Council meeting, I outlined the nature of Turkey's relations and cooperation with the countries of the region, including Syria. In light of the remarks made by the representative of Israel during his takeout today and this meeting, I believe it will be useful to reiterate those points. First and foremost, strengthening its national capacities is a sovereign right of Syria. It does not constitute a threat to any country, and it is not any business of Israel. Turkey's relations with the countries of the region, including Syria, are guided by our firm commitment to their stability, security, and prosperity. We regard these three elements as indispensable, not only for our own national security, but also for regional and international security. A shared commitment to these objectives by all countries would make a significant contribution to lasting peace and stability in the region. Conversely, attempts to obstruct Syria's efforts to build and strengthen its security capacity would only risk creating conditions conducive to the resurgence of terrorist organizations such as Daesh. Against this background, we categorically reject Israel's attempts to smear Turkey's legitimate cooperation with Syria and portray it as a threat in an effort to justify its own violations of international law. Turkey's military cooperation with Syria is conducted with the consent of the sovereign Syrian government. None of our activities in Syria are directed against or pose a threat to any third country. In this regard, Israeli attempts to draw parallels between its decades-long occupation of Syrian territory and Turkey's legitimate security cooperation with the Syrian government are entirely groundless. Mr. President, unfortunately, Israeli representative went beyond all red lines against my country and President. Indeed, answers to his questions are clear. What is the difference between Israel and Turkey? because Turkey is a friend of Syria, contrary to Israel. Turkey is a deep-rooted, responsible state, contrary to Israel, which is an aggressive state in the Middle East to many countries. Turkey's friendship to Israel, Turkey's care about Syria, and Turkey's care about Syrian people and Syrian stability was well-proven during decade of conflict and in the post-conflict. by protecting Syrian people within Turkey and within Syria, and by helping to rebuild modern Syria after revolution, after post-conflict. So, Mr. President, such distortions in this Council had been made before by the regime of -- by the representative of former regime against my country's presence and my country's role in Syria. It is a pity that Israel representative took over that role, volunteered to that role. So I reject all his baseless claims. Turkish role in any part of the region, Turkish role has always been positive, constructive, and it deserves just a thank you from everybody, but I don't expect it from Israel. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Turkey for his statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Oman.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of the Arab Group in New York during this monthly meeting of the Council on the agenda item, the situation in the Middle East. The Arab Group expresses its thanks and appreciation to all briefers. The Arab Group also reiterates once again its firm support of the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab Republic. We remain committed to Syria's security and stability. The Arab Group underscores the importance of supporting efforts aimed at stability and preserving the Syrian state institutions and creating the conducive conditions for recovery and reconstruction. We reaffirm that the unity and stability of Syria constitute a cornerstone of security and stability in the region. Mr. President, the Arab Group strongly condemns the Israeli attacks and incursions into Syrian territory, including the attack against the Al-Buhair airport. These actions constitute a violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, and they are a blatant attempt to fuel strife and to threat efforts aimed at de-escalation and stability. We also condemn the unlawful entry of Israeli officials into Syrian territory. We call for enforcing Israel to respect the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and to refrain from any measure that could increase tensions or impose new facts on the ground. The Arab Group further reaffirms that the Syrian Golan is occupied Arab Syrian territory and stresses the need to respect the relevant resolutions, most important among which is Security Council Resolution 497 of 1981. The resolution has determined that Israel's imposition of its laws with jurisdiction and administration in the Golan is null and void and without legal effect. Mr. President, the Arab Group condemns the measures taken by -- commends, rather, commends the Syrian efforts to counter terrorist groups and maintain security and stability. And we affirm the importance of supporting these efforts The Arab Group stresses the importance of continuing counterterrorism efforts and to prevent the return of terrorists in any form. We reiterate the need to respect international law and all Security Council resolutions on counterterrorism. The Arab Group also welcomes the continued cooperation between the Syrian Government and the United Nations and its specialized agencies. This cooperation is an important avenue for supporting stability and meeting humanitarian and development needs. Mr. President, the Arab Group calls for providing international support and investment and strengthening economic cooperation to serve the economic recovery and reconstruction efforts and create the appropriate conditions for the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of refugees and IDPs, including through providing services, infrastructure, livelihoods, and mine clearance. In the same context, the Arab Group commends the great role of host countries in hosting Syrian refugees, and we call on the international community to increase support directed to host countries who cannot bear this burden alone on behalf of the international community until the return of refugees to their homeland. The group also encourages the continued work on the issues related to missing persons, accountability, and national reconciliation in order to enhance confidence and long-term stability. In conclusion, we call on the Security Council to adopt a balanced and constructive approach based on respect for Syria's sovereignty and to reject any steps that will undermine stability, and also to support economic and humanitarian recovery in order to serve the interests of the Syrian people and contribute to the stability and security of the region. Thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the representative of Oman for that statement on behalf of the Arab group. The representative of the Syrian Arab Republic has asked for the floor for another statement, and I give him the floor for another statement. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. I will not address my remarks directly permanent representative of Israel, because I assume it must be outrageous for him to come here, being asked to come here again to try and mend losses internationally when for one person's dreams domestically after every time he breaches Syrian sovereignty. But perhaps let me address several of the points made. On the questions of buffers and on the point of refreshing memories, you may recall that when Israel occupied the Golan Heights illegally, which as colleagues mentioned in Resolution 497, said was not on void. It was said that it was a buffer that Israel wanted to protect itself. And so what is happening now is not for military or security reasons. The map shown by the permanent representative does not include the buffer they previously occupied, allegedly to protect themselves. But assuming there might be security concerns, on day one, after the massive change that he talked about, We immediately engaged with the United States and opened bold talks that never happened before in Syria's history in that way. And we said we're ready for mediation to reach a security agreement. There was no proper answer. But we're not talking about breaches of sovereignty and territorial integrity only. I can quote from the ONDOP report, the breaches to the 1974 agreement. I can quote from the oral update of the UN Commission of Inquiry that went into the south of Syria and reported several times in its statements, and I have quotations here, about the war crimes being committed by Israel against Syrians. Ongoing violations, and I quote, of Syrian sovereignty, along with reported violations of international humanitarian law, including those that may amount to war crimes, have severe implications on the rights of the affected civilian populations. With the fall of the Assad regime, Mr. President, we thought the era for commissions of inquiry and war crimes and crimes against humanity was over. It seems we were wrong. On the points of communities and resilience, some of their officials tried to reach out to Syrian Kurds. They rejected them, integrated within the Syrian government. Responsible Syrian Druze did the same. They're in parliament. They accepted security positions. They rejected foreign support. And those of them who drew figures who, as you've heard today from Mr. Kordoni, dare to speak against one faction backed by Israel, get expelled out of Sweden. Even Syrian Jews, Mr. President, run for parliament in Syria. They're back renovating their synagogues. So this is the Syria we are building. And when it comes to the military presence in Syria, again, I'm assuming these questions were asked upon him to deliver them because I know of his legal credentials and he understands the difference between consent of one state or the other and our ability to decide to choose who we're working with. We didn't hear complaints when we chose to join the US-led coalition against ISIS. That was a military cooperation that happened with so many of you in Syria. The same happened with other countries here around the council, where we're constantly engaging in military deals, opening doors, and so on. And so if it is about one specific situation, please do not bring it to this council. Syria's meeting should not be talking about proxy issues anymore. That was the case during the regime era. It should no longer be the case. It's frankly traumatizing. But even Israeli figures, opposition figures, think tanks, are telling that this Israeli government is missing out an opportunity to show the world that when there is no credible threat and there is mediation efforts ongoing, that Israel will behave differently than in other parts of the region. I think the whole world has seen what has happened. Time is running out, Mr. President, but just not yet. And we will continue to engage with the bold actions of President Trump in mediation efforts in a way that does not jeopardize the rights of Syrian civilians, nor legitimize occupation. And until then, colleagues, we will continue to build and build and move ahead with the things that all of you have praised to build the Syria that is worthy of its history for its future. Thank you.

Arab Republic for the statement. And the representative of Israel has asked for the floor for a further statement, and I give the floor for the last statement.

First of all, Ambassador Olabi, nobody asked me to come and speak here today. Actually, it's because of your actions that I'm here, because I watched your stakeout the other day, and I saw how much attention you pay towards Israel in all of those discussions that you have here in this council, and I decided that I have to come and ask the questions. And I think that I'm still waiting for answers about what I raised regarding Turkey and about what we learned from Lebanon, Because today, we are paying a heavy price fighting the radicals in Lebanon. And we want to see an independent Lebanon. And one thing we all want to avoid is to see that Lebanon was not the last country that has been taken by other countries in the region. So I believe me when I tell you we do want to see independent Syria, like we want to see independent Lebanon. But we look at what's happening in Syria, we look at the actions, not the declarations. When it comes to the minorities, to the Druze minority, we have seen the roadmap and we have read the reports that you're not fulfilling the roadmap. I'm not looking for more reasons to come here. And many, many countries in history like to blame Israel for their own problems. Thank you.
